Let me lay down some background here. We're a new group of players and DM, all fresh (except for one guy who played a few years ago). For the past two weeks I've built a homebrew campaign, and messed around with the basic rules to get more simplified mechanics. It hasn't worked out too well so far, and because we tried different DMs and one guy left we've got a handful of unused PCs, but I'm still trying. Also, one of the guys is a pseudo-DM: while I can world-build and create a story/dungeon like no other, he can improv like Jim Carrey.

So tonight's session was a little interesting. The party learned about a young dragon in the mountains nearby that's been terrorizing the nearby farmers. After a bit of navigation, they end up at the dragon's cave. A couple puzzles later, they arrive at the dragon, who was eying them rather hungrily. Luckily, one PC had a dragon figurine earlier (which was enchanted to boost relationships with dragons), and actually managed to tame it! After a short discussion, translating through one NPC who spoke draconic, they convinced the dragon to follow them to a nicer cave. Well, a couple crit 1s during perception checks and the party ended up blind. That's ok, the aforementioned NPC can lead them!

...Except he's a dunderhead. They ended up in the middle of a desert with only one city nearby, and no dragon to be seen. When they arrived at the city, they discover it's the main location of the BBEG's army! They promptly got captured, and met up with some previous PCs that were now NPCs. They managed to convince the slaves to start a revolution, and make their escape. It all ended with an epic clash between the slaves and the prison garrison. With a few lucky rolls they actually managed to overwhelm the guards and make an escape.

It's been the best session so far, and proof that I want to keep doing this. Thanks to you guys and those who switched from r/DnD to over here, it's been a lot of help reading all the discussions!

Semi-related fun fact - the term 'cracker' originally had nothing to do with slavery or whips, it was a term coined in the British isles to describe lower class 'braggarts' that were quick to crack back with a witty retort. The first settlers in Florida after the British obtained it from the Spanish were mainly from this group of British/Irish/Scottish/Welsh people, who largely became cattle wranglers who were too poor to afford slaves. It being used to describe general white people and it having the connotation of those who formerly lashed slaves with whips is a modern invention.

ELI5: Why Did Users Leave Digg?

They changed their whole website to a " follow" site instead of a "vote" site. At the same time they also implemented Facebook and Twitter integration and people didn't like that stuff back then. They also got more and more sponsored content.

Reddit was rising in popularity already in those days, their cleaner and simpler interface probably made the new Digg users stay there.

The two main reasons was the lack of or removal of compelling content ( interesting links or discussion) and a reformatting of the ways in which content could reach the front page, all of this was done to be more marketable to advertisers and companies willing to pay for placement of articles.

It didn't help that for a while something like less than 2-3% of submitters were responsible for 90% or more of the front page, being able to direct huge volumes of internet traffic and view counts though digg meant that there was a monetary factor in remaining in control of the front page and then it was soon realized that controlling the comments was also a way that astroturfing (pretending to be legitimate person(s) with an opinion but really a paid stooge for a company etc ) companies could promote all kinds of things so there was a lot of digg up and bury manipulation in the comments sections. Instead of combating this and trying to even the playing field for standard users the changes made to digg were nothing but an attempt to wrestle control of this front page control away from 3rd parties and users in order to start profiting directly from it.

Some would say Reddit appears to be trying to do something very similar and a few former 4chan users would say that Moot (owner of 4chan) was attempting something like this.
